findings.paper_title: Joint Half Year TM Outturn Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Both councils have complied with all the Treasury Management Indicators for the first half of 2026/27.
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer reports that treasury activity complied with the CIPFA Code and the approved strategy, and that all treasury management indicators were met. Mid Suffolk's external borrowing sat within its £230m authorised limit and £215m operational boundary at 30 September 2026.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can use the report's compliance statement and limit figures as a reference point for their own indicator reporting.
findings.figures: Mid Suffolk external borrowing £98,194k at 30 September 2026 against an authorised limit of £230,000k and operational boundary of £215,000k
findings.quote: Both Councils have complied with all the Treasury Management Indicators for the period

findings.paper_title: Joint Half Year TM Outturn Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Mid Suffolk's HRA capital financing requirement is forecast to rise from £129.0m at 31 March 2026 to £140.5m at 31 March 2027.
findings.detail: The paper's Table 1 shows the HRA CFR increasing by £11.5m in the year, while the General Fund CFR falls by £1.7m. Total external borrowing for Mid Suffolk is forecast to reach £123.4m at 31 March 2027 against £92.8m at 31 March 2026.
findings.matters: Growth in the HRA's need to borrow, funded by tenant rents, is a long-term commitment that a lender or finance director would weigh against future rent income.
findings.figures: HRA CFR £129,019k at 31 March 2026 and £140,548k forecast at 31 March 2027 (movement £11,529k); Mid Suffolk external borrowing £92,786k at 31 March 2026 and £123,373k forecast at 31 March 2027

findings.paper_title: Joint Half Year TM Outturn Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Phase two of the Mid Suffolk Growth Ltd Needham Market housing scheme was cancelled, with £877k of costs written off in 2025/26, and the phase two land has been sold for £2,7m.
findings.detail: Phase one of the joint venture generated a £321k land receipt and a £281k dividend for the council. The paper says phase two land has now been sold by the council, and the development agreement is due to be formally closed in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A cancelled housing phase with written-off costs, followed by a land sale, shows the realised outcome of a council-backed development that a peer council could compare with its own joint ventures.
findings.figures: Phase two costs written off £877k (2025/26); phase two land sale £2,7m (as written); phase one land receipt £321k; phase one dividend £281k
findings.quote: Phase two of the development has been cancelled, having incurred costs of £877k which were written off in the 2025/26 Statement of Accounts.

findings.paper_title: Joint Half Year TM Outturn Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Gateway 14 Ltd will pay no further interest to Mid Suffolk, moving to dividends, with a £2.9m dividend forecast for 2026/27.
findings.detail: Mid Suffolk has received £5m of interest from Gateway 14 since the loans were advanced. The company received £6m of dividends in 2025/26, and the paper expects future returns to come through dividend income rather than interest.
findings.matters: A change from interest to dividend income changes how the return is recognised, and this affects the income line a finance director forecasts against.
findings.figures: Interest received £5m since loans were advanced; dividend received £6m in 2025/26; forecast dividend £2.9m for 2026/27
findings.quote: Going forward, no further interest income will be receivable from Gateway 14 Ltd, as the company has transitioned from paying interest to issuing dividends.

findings.paper_title: Joint Half Year TM Outturn Report 2026.27
findings.headline: CIFCO Capital Ltd has deferred £1.3m of interest to date, and its business plan permits a 10% deferment of interest repayments to aid cashflow.
findings.detail: The paper says CIFCO pays interest in arrears and that its business plan allows a 10% deferment while sales and works are delivered. Mid Suffolk and Babergh each hold loans of £42.8m with CIFCO, and the expected credit loss on those loans was £434k at 31 March 2026.
findings.matters: Interest deferral by a council-owned company converts income the council has earned into a receivable, and a finance director at another council with a similar company structure would want to see the scale of that deferral.
findings.figures: Interest deferred to date £1 .3m (as written); loans to CIFCO £42.8m per council at 30 September 2026; expected credit loss £434k at 31 March 2026; interest received £14.9m excluding deferments
findings.quote: The total interest deferred to date is £1 .3m.

findings.paper_title: Joint Half Year TM Outturn Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Mid Suffolk's General Fund financing costs are forecast to rise from £1.8m in 2025/26 to £2.9m in 2026/27, from 10% to 14% of net revenue stream.
findings.detail: The paper's prudential indicators show General Fund financing costs (interest plus MRP charged to revenue) increasing in 2026/27 and continuing to rise to 2028/29. The paper presents these as forecasts and budgets.
findings.matters: A rising share of net revenue absorbed by financing costs is the measure a finance director or lender uses to judge how much room the general fund has for other spending.
findings.figures: General Fund financing costs £1,768k (2025/26 actual), £2,879k (2026/27 forecast), £3,808k (2027/28 budget), £3,920k (2028/29 budget); proportion of net revenue stream 10%, 14%, 19%, 20%

findings.paper_title: Joint Half Year TM Outturn Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing from other local authorities cost 3.8% to 5.5% during the period, with costs rising throughout it.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the high short-term cost mainly to many authorities avoiding more expensive long-term rates and relying more on the short-term market, with low cash levels and non-receipt of SEND grants also contributing. Over the same period, PWLB 20-year maturity rates moved from 6.13% to 6.61%.
findings.matters: Councils replacing maturing or called debt in the short-term market are paying these rates, so the figures are a direct benchmark for the cost of replacement funding.
findings.figures: Short-term local authority borrowing 3.8% to 5.5%; PWLB 20-year maturity rate 6.13% to 6.61%; Mid Suffolk average short term borrowing rate 4.51% at 30/09/26 (Table 2)
findings.quote: The cost of short-term borrowing from other local authorities has been above Bank Rate during the period at 3.8% to 5.5%: costs have risen throughout the period.

findings.paper_title: Joint Half Year TM Outturn Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Mid Suffolk's total borrowing rose by £5.4m in the first half of 2026/27 to £98.1m at 30 September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper reports that Mid Suffolk's loans increased over the six months, while Babergh's decreased. The increase follows the LOBO repayment and a rise in short term borrowing from other local authorities.
findings.matters: A finance director tracking debt growth against the budgeted borrowing path can see the half-year movement directly.
findings.figures: £98.1m loans at 30 September 2026; increase of £5.4m since 31 March 2026; total borrowing £92,786k at 31 March 2026 and £98,194k at 30 September 2026
findings.quote: On 30 September 2026 Babergh held £121.3m of loans, a decrease of £2.2m and Mid Suffolk held £98.1m of loans, an increase of £5.4m since 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Joint Half Year TM Outturn Report 2026.27
findings.headline: Mid Suffolk has paid off £4m of LOBO loans from Dexia Credit Local, where the lender was proposing an increase in interest rates during 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper says the council repaid the £4m of LOBO borrowing in the first half, after the lender proposed a rate increase. The paper does not state the proposed rate, the original maturity of the loans, or the cost of the replacement funding.
findings.matters: A LOBO call is a repayment and replacement event, so the council had to find £4m of cash and replacement funding, and a finance director at another council holding similar LOBOs can compare this outcome with their own.
findings.figures: LOBO balance £4.0m at 31 March 2026, nil at 30 September 2026; LOBO average rate 4.21% at 30/09/26 (Table 2); Mid Suffolk short term borrowing from local authorities £5.0m at 31 March 2026 and £15.0m at 30 September 2026
findings.quote: Mid Suffolk has now paid off £4m of LOBO (Lender’s Option Borrower’s Option) loans where the lender, Dexia Credit Local, was proposing an increase in the interest rates during 2026/27.

findings.detail: This was the position reported in November 2025. The follow-up says the workflow recommendations are now implemented, and the reporting recommendation remains open.
findings.matters: A system-level gap that stops journal samples being drawn is one a finance director at another council running Unit 4 would want to check against their own set-up.

findings.headline: The journals follow-up review found two of three November 2025 recommendations fully implemented, with the Unit 4 standardised journal reporting recommendation still open against a revised implementation date.

news_drafts.headline: Mid Suffolk repays £4m of LOBO loans after lender proposed a higher interest rate
news_drafts.lead:
Mid Suffolk District Council repaid £4m of LOBO loans in the first half of 2026/27, after the lender, Dexia Credit Local, proposed an increase in the interest rate. A LOBO loan is a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it. The council's joint half-year treasury management report says Mid Suffolk "has now paid off" the loans.

The report's figures show the council's LOBO borrowing at £4.0m on 31 March 2026 and nil on 30 September 2026. Over the same six months, its short-term borrowing from other local authorities rose from £5.0m to £15.0m.

The paper does not state the rate the lender proposed, the original maturity of the loans or the cost of any replacement funding. The report is before the Joint Audit and Standards Committee on 30 November 2026.
